learn.title: The merge step as code
learn.body: Merge sort rests on one function: merge two sorted arrays into a third. It uses three indexes, `i` for the first array, `j` for the second and `k` for the output.

learn.title: merge
learn.body: The first loop takes the smaller front item. The last two loops copy whatever is left over in one array.

learn.title: Merge {1, 4, 7} and {2, 3, 9}
steps: 1 and 2: take 1. Then 4 and 2: take 2. Then 4 and 3: take 3
The first array is used up, so the last loop copies 9

learn.title: Cost of merging
learn.body: Every comparison places one item in `out`, and the leftover copies place the rest. So merging n items in total takes at most n - 1 comparisons and exactly n items are written: $O(n)$. It needs an extra array of size n for the output.

learn.title: Why <= and not <
learn.body: When two items are equal we take the one from the first array. That keeps equal items in their original order. This property is called stability, and the next lesson explains why it matters.
Check both arrays are used up. The two copy loops handle the case where one array ends before the other.

questions.prompt: What do the indexes `i`, `j` and `k` track?
choices: Position in the first array, the second array and the output
questions.explanation: `i` and `j` walk the inputs while `k` writes the output.

questions.prompt: Merge {1, 4, 7} and {2, 3, 9}. What is the 3rd item of the output?
questions.explanation: The output is 1 2 3 4 7 9, so the third item is 3.

questions.prompt: When the first array runs out, what happens?
choices: The remaining items of the second array are copied
questions.explanation: The second array is already sorted, so its leftovers go straight to the end.

questions.prompt: Merging two sorted arrays of total length n takes \_\_ time.
questions.explanation: Each item is placed once, in a single pass.

questions.prompt: Merge {1, 3, 5, 7} and {2, 4, 6, 8}, taking the smaller front each time. How many comparisons are made?
questions.explanation: The fronts alternate between the two arrays, and the last item needs no comparison: 8 items, 7 comparisons.

choices: Copies `a[i]` to `out[k]`, then moves both indexes on
questions.explanation: Post-increment uses the old value of the index and then adds one.

questions.prompt: Put the merge loop steps in order.
steps: Advance the index of the array used and `k`
Copy leftovers once one array is empty
questions.explanation: Compare, copy, advance, then handle leftovers at the end.
